title: THE KING WHO WAS SHOT THROUGH THE HEART… AND THROWN INTO A FIELD WHERE GOD HAD BEEN WAITING FOR HIM
paragraphs: THE KING WHO WAS SHOT THROUGH THE HEART… AND THROWN INTO A FIELD WHERE GOD HAD BEEN WAITING FOR HIM

He wore a crown. He commanded an army. He thought he was chasing an enemy. But one arrow exposed a judgment that had been waiting for years. And what happened to his body reveals a terrifying truth about sin, a breathtaking truth about God's justice, and the only hope any of us have in Jesus Christ.
“And Jehu drew a bow with his full strength, and smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot.” — 2 Kings 9:24, KJV
There are some places you can leave behind without ever really escaping what happened there.
A house where someone betrayed you.
A room where your innocence was taken.
A family table where everybody pretended nothing was wrong.
A field where an innocent man lost everything because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
Years pass. People die. New rulers take their places. The world moves on.
And eventually, someone begins to believe that what happened has been forgotten.
But there is something terrifying about the story you are about to read.
A king was riding through the countryside, completely unaware that the ground beneath him was connected to a crime committed by his own family.
He had horses. Soldiers. Authority. A throne waiting for him.
But he was about to discover that a crown cannot protect a man from the judgment of God.
An arrow would enter his body.
His chariot would become the place of his death.
And his corpse would be thrown into a field.
Not just any field.
The very field connected to the blood his father had shed.
And the most chilling part?
God had spoken about that field years before the king ever arrived there.
Stay with this story, because the arrow is not the deepest part.
The field is.
And beyond that field is a question every human heart must eventually answer.
What happens when the sins we thought were buried finally come into the light?
His name was Joram, also called Jehoram, king of Israel.
He was the son of Ahab.
And if you know anything about Ahab and Jezebel, you know this family carried a terrible history.
But to understand why Joram's body ended up in a field, we must return to a moment when another man was still alive.
His name was Naboth.
Naboth owned a vineyard in Jezreel.
It was not merely a piece of real estate. It was his ancestral inheritance, something deeply connected to the covenant life of Israel and the land passed down through generations.
King Ahab wanted it.
He offered Naboth money or another vineyard in exchange.
But Naboth refused.
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.” — 1 Kings 21:3, KJV
Naboth was not being disrespectful.
He was honoring an inheritance that mattered before God.
But Ahab did not like being told no.
Imagine that.
A king who possessed enormous wealth, servants, influence, and military power became miserable because one ordinary man would not surrender a small piece of land.
Ahab went home, lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel entered the story.
She saw her husband's disappointment and decided that the problem could be solved.
Not through negotiation.
Not through justice.
Through murder disguised as righteousness.
She arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of blaspheming God and the king.
A fast was proclaimed. A public proceeding was staged. Religious language became a weapon against an innocent man.
And Naboth was taken outside the city and stoned to death.
Read that slowly.
An innocent man was murdered through a conspiracy that pretended to defend the honor of God.
And afterward, Ahab went down to take possession of the vineyard.
The man was dead.
The property was available.
The powerful had won.
At least, that is how it looked.
But heaven had witnessed everything.
The false testimony.
The abuse of authority.
The bloodshed.
The theft.
The terrible silence after the crowd went home.
And God sent Elijah with a message.
“Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” — 1 Kings 21:19, KJV
What a question.
You killed him.
And now you are taking what belonged to him?
God was not confused about the transaction.
He saw the murder behind the ownership.
He saw the injustice behind the royal privilege.
And He announced judgment against Ahab's house.
But something unexpected happened.
Ahab humbled himself.
He tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and walked in mourning.
And God took notice.
In 1 Kings 21:29, the Lord declared that because Ahab had humbled himself, the announced disaster against his house would not come during Ahab's lifetime but during his son's days.
Do not miss this.
Even in a story filled with corruption, God noticed an act of humility.
That did not erase the consequences of Ahab's evil.
It did not make Naboth's murder acceptable.
But it revealed something about the God of Scripture.
He is not indifferent to repentance.
And He is never obligated to ignore justice.
Years passed.
Ahab died.
His son Joram eventually became king.
And the old prophecy continued moving toward fulfillment.
By the time we reach 2 Kings 9, Joram had been wounded in battle against the Arameans and was recovering at Jezreel.
Meanwhile, Jehu, a military commander, had been anointed king through a messenger sent by the prophet Elisha.
Jehu was commissioned to execute judgment against Ahab's dynasty.
Then came the ride toward Jezreel.
A watchman saw Jehu's company approaching.
Messengers were sent to ask whether he came in peace.
They did not return.
Finally, Joram ordered his chariot prepared.
He rode out to meet Jehu.
Ahaziah, king of Judah, went with him.
And then Scripture includes one detail that should make the reader stop.
“And they went out against him, and met him in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite.” — 2 Kings 9:21, KJV
There it was.
Naboth's land.
The ground associated with the injustice of Ahab's house.
The place where a man had lost his inheritance because powerful people had decided his life was expendable.
Joram did not know how the encounter would end.
But the reader has already been told enough to recognize the significance of the location.
He asked Jehu a question.
“Is it peace, Jehu?” — 2 Kings 9:22, KJV
And Jehu answered:
“What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?”
The language is severe because the confrontation is severe.

In the biblical context, Jezebel's influence included idolatry and practices condemned under Israel's covenant with God. The accusation concerns a kingdom corrupted by persistent rebellion against the Lord.
Joram understood the danger.
He turned his chariot and fled, warning Ahaziah:
“There is treachery, O Ahaziah.”
Then Jehu drew his bow.
Scripture says he drew it with his full strength.
The Hebrew expression in 2 Kings 9:24 is:
מִלֵּא יָדוֹ בַקֶּשֶׁת
Millēʾ yādô baqqešet.
Literally, the expression describes filling his hand with the bow, an idiom understood in context as drawing or handling the bow with full force.
It emphasizes the deliberate action of the archer.
This was not a stray arrow in the confusion of battle.
Jehu aimed.
He released.
And the arrow struck Joram between the shoulders, passing through his heart.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיֵּצֵא הַחֵצִי מִלִּבּוֹ
Vayyēṣēʾ haḥēṣî millibbô.
“And the arrow came out from his heart.”
The king collapsed in his chariot.
The man who had ridden out demanding to know whether there was peace was dead.
His horses could still move.
His chariot still existed.
His title had not vanished from the historical record.
But none of those things could give him another heartbeat.
And then came the command that makes this account unforgettable.
Jehu turned to Bidkar, his officer, and ordered him to take Joram's body and throw it into the portion of Naboth's field.
Why?
Because Jehu remembered the word of the Lord spoken against Ahab.
He recalled that he and Bidkar had been riding behind Ahab when the prophetic judgment was pronounced.
Then Jehu quoted the divine declaration:
“Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the LORD; and I will requite thee in this plat, saith the LORD.” — 2 Kings 9:26, KJV
Notice those words.
“I have seen.”
The Hebrew reads:
אִם־לֹא אֶת־דְּמֵי נָבוֹת וְאֶת־דְּמֵי בָנָיו רָאִיתִי אֶמֶשׁ
ʾIm-lōʾ ʾet-demê Nābôt weʾet-demê bānāyw rāʾîtî ʾemeš.
The force of the oath is that the Lord had certainly seen the blood of Naboth and his sons.
The Hebrew word רָאִיתִי (rāʾîtî) means “I saw” or “I have seen.”
And דְּמֵי (demê) is the plural construct form of “blood,” used here in the expression referring to bloodshed.

There is a textual detail worth understanding: 2 Kings 9:26 mentions Naboth's sons, while the account in 1 Kings 21 focuses on Naboth's murder without narrating the deaths of his sons. The later passage supplies that additional detail without explaining the circumstances.
The Bible does not invite us to invent a scene that it does not describe.
But it does tell us that God saw the blood.
The crime had not disappeared simply because the people who committed it had moved on.
The field had not forgotten its history in the eyes of the Lord.
And the royal family could not erase God's testimony.
Joram's body was thrown into Naboth's portion of land.
A king ended up lifeless in the place associated with a man his family had wronged.
No royal ceremony is described.
No magnificent procession.
No final speech.
Just a dead king.
A field.
And the fulfillment of a divine word.
Now consider something that makes this story more uncomfortable than many of us want to admit.
Joram was not Ahab.
He did not personally arrange the conspiracy against Naboth in the account of 1 Kings 21.
Yet he belonged to the dynasty under judgment, and Scripture also describes him as continuing in evil, though not in precisely the same manner as his father and mother (2 Kings 3:2–3).
This is not permission for us to punish children for their parents' crimes.
Deuteronomy 24:16 explicitly rejects that practice in Israel's human courts, and Ezekiel 18 teaches personal responsibility before God.
The judgment in 2 Kings 9 belongs to a particular prophetic and covenantal history, not a general rule that descendants should suffer violence for ancestral wrongdoing.
But it does confront us with a truth we cannot escape.
Sin does not always stop hurting people when the person who began it is gone.
A father's cruelty can leave wounds in his children.
A mother's deception can become a pattern repeated in the family.
A leader's corruption can poison a community long after that leader dies.
And what one generation excuses, another generation may learn to normalize.
Perhaps that is why this ancient story can feel painfully modern.
Because not every stolen vineyard looks like a vineyard.
Sometimes it is a reputation destroyed by a lie.
Sometimes it is an inheritance taken through manipulation.
Sometimes it is a worker cheated by someone who knows that the worker cannot afford to fight back.
Sometimes it is a child silenced to protect the image of an adult.
Sometimes it is a church member wounded by a leader who knows how to quote Scripture but refuses to practice justice.
And sometimes the hardest part is not what happened.
It is watching the people responsible continue living as though nothing happened at all.
You wonder whether God noticed.
You wonder whether your tears mattered.
You wonder whether truth will ever come out.
Naboth's story reminds us that God is not blind to injustice.
But we must be careful here.
It does not promise that every wrong will be publicly exposed during our lifetime.
It does not promise that every abuser will fall in a dramatic confrontation.
And it certainly does not authorize us to become Jehu, take vengeance into our own hands, or treat our anger as a divine commission.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
God's justice is not a license for our cruelty.
It is a reason to entrust ultimate judgment to Him while pursuing truth, protection, accountability, and lawful justice where we can.
And there is another danger in this story.
It is easy to read about Ahab and Jezebel and think only about the people who hurt us.
It is easy to see ourselves as Naboth.
The wounded one.
The betrayed one.
The one who lost something.
But what happens when the Holy Spirit turns the light toward us?
What if there are moments when we have been Ahab?
Wanting something so badly that we resented the person who stood in our way.
What if there are moments when we have been Jezebel?
Using pressure, manipulation, falsehood, or spiritual language to control an outcome.
What if we have been Joram?
Comfortable inside patterns of sin that we inherited, defended, or refused to confront.
Not every sin is murder.
Not every failure is equivalent in seriousness.
But every one of us has reason to examine our own heart before the holiness of God.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That includes the person who wounded you.
And it includes you.
It includes me.
And suddenly, the field becomes more than the location of a king's death.
It becomes a mirror.
Because the question is no longer simply whether God saw what someone else did.
The question is what God has seen in us.
The private compromises.
The jealousy we dressed up as concern.
The bitterness we fed in silence.
The apology we never offered.
The truth we twisted because honesty would have cost us something.
The sin we kept calling a struggle while secretly making room for it.
God sees.
Not because He delights in humiliating sinners.
But because nothing is hidden from the One who is perfectly holy.
Hebrews 4:13 says that all things are naked and opened before the eyes of Him with whom we have to do.
And if the story ended there, we would have reason to tremble.
Because Joram's story reminds us that judgment is real.
But the Gospel announces something Joram's field could never accomplish.
There is a King who did not come to escape judgment, but to bear the judgment His people deserved.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story takes a turn no human imagination could have earned.
Joram was a king whose heart was pierced by an arrow.
Jesus was the King whose side was pierced after His death on the cross.
John 19:34 tells us that a soldier pierced His side with a spear, and blood and water came out.
These are different events, with different meanings. Scripture does not explicitly identify Joram's death as a prophecy of Christ's crucifixion.
But the contrast is worth contemplating.
Joram's death was part of the judgment against a corrupt royal house.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Joram could not save himself from the arrow.
Jesus did not save Himself from the cross, though He had the authority to lay down His life and take it up again (John 10:17–18).
Joram's body was cast into a field associated with injustice.
Jesus' body was laid in a new tomb in a garden, according to John 19:41–42.
And unlike Joram, Jesus did not remain dead.
On the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection is not a poetic way of saying that His influence survived.
It is the Christian proclamation that the crucified Christ truly conquered death.
And that changes everything.
Because the same God who sees the blood of the innocent also sees the blood of His Son.
The blood of Naboth cried out as evidence of injustice.
The blood of Jesus is the blood of the new covenant, shed for the forgiveness of sins.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus as the mediator of the new covenant and of His sprinkled blood, which speaks better things than the blood of Abel.
The point is not that God stopped caring about justice.
The point is that, through Jesus Christ, God provides a righteous way to forgive sinners without pretending that sin is harmless.
Romans 3:25–26 presents Christ as the One through whom God demonstrates His righteousness, so that He is both just and the justifier of the person who has faith in Jesus.
Think about that.
God does not look at your sin and call it beautiful.
He does not call betrayal faithfulness.
He does not call abuse love.
He does not call pride humility.
He does not pretend that darkness is light.
But in Christ, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and a new life to people who could never make themselves righteous.
That is grace.
Not God ignoring evil.
Not God lowering His holiness.
Not God declaring that the damage we caused never mattered.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God given through the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And repentance is not an attempt to purchase that mercy.
It is the fitting response of a heart turning away from sin and toward the Savior.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent or change one's mind.
Biblical repentance is more than an emotional moment.
It involves a changed orientation toward God and sin, with a life that increasingly bears fruit consistent with that change.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Notice that He did not say, “Hide your past until you become acceptable.”
He called people to turn and believe.
The cross is where the guilty can find forgiveness.
The resurrection is where the hopeless can find living hope.
And the Holy Spirit begins the work of transformation in those who belong to Christ.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message for people who have never entered a church.
It is for the father who knows he has wounded his family.
The mother who is exhausted from pretending to be strong.
The young person carrying shame over a secret.
The church leader who needs to stop defending an image and start telling the truth.
The believer who has become cold, distracted, proud, or spiritually numb.
And the wounded person who wonders whether God has forgotten the injustice done to them.
Jesus does not ask the wounded to pretend their wounds are imaginary.
And He does not invite the guilty to hide behind religious performance.
He calls us into truth.
For some, that means repentance and confession.
For others, it means receiving comfort, seeking safety, and beginning the difficult journey of healing.
For those who have harmed others, genuine repentance may require restitution, accountability, and accepting consequences.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust or remove the need for justice.
But no life is beyond the reach of Christ's transforming power simply because its story contains scandal.
And perhaps that is the part you needed to hear.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The shame you carry does not have to be your permanent identity.
The sin you have confessed does not have to remain your master.
The wound someone gave you does not have to define the whole of your future.
Because Jesus Christ does more than offer a new public image.
He gives new life.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Not a better disguise.
Not a more religious mask.
A new creation.
And if you are reading this with something heavy on your conscience, perhaps you already know what needs to change.
There is a conversation you have been avoiding.
A sin you have been rationalizing.
A relationship where you need to tell the truth.
A hidden habit that is slowly stealing your peace.
A wound you need help carrying rather than continuing to bury.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval.
Second Peter 3:9 describes His patience as connected to His desire that people come to repentance.
Today is not an invitation to panic.
It is an invitation to return.
You do not need to wait until an arrow strikes your life before you take God's Word seriously.
You do not need to reach the end of yourself before admitting that you need a Savior.
You can come to Jesus now.
Not with a perfect speech.
Not with an impressive religious résumé.
But with faith, repentance, and a heart willing to surrender.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have done, what I have hidden, what I have suffered, and what I have become. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from sin and trust You. Heal what is broken in me. Give me courage to tell the truth, make right what I can, and follow You even when obedience costs me something. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
Open your Bible.
Read the Gospel of John.
Find a faithful, Scripture-teaching local church.
Speak with a mature Christian who can help you grow in the faith.
If you need to confess a wrong, seek wise and appropriate accountability.
If you have been harmed, reach out to trustworthy people who can help protect and support you.
And keep walking with Christ.
Because discipleship is not one dramatic moment followed by a lifetime of spiritual neglect.
It is a daily life of abiding in the One who saved us.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish stories that make people feel something for a few minutes.
But to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, examine their lives honestly, and grow in Jesus Christ.
We want the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church to know that the invitation of Christ is real.
We want the exhausted believer to find encouragement rooted in God's Word.
We want families to open the Bible together.
We want those who have grown spiritually cold to rediscover the seriousness and beauty of following Jesus.
And we want people who have been wounded by sin to know that the Gospel offers more than condemnation or empty reassurance.
It offers the living Savior.
You do not need to reveal private details or tell strangers something that would put you at risk.
But perhaps you can simply write:
Or if you are weary but still holding on to faith:
“I'm still fighting. Pray for me.”
And if Christ has already begun restoring something you once thought was beyond repair, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness.
Someone reading the comments may be struggling to believe that change is possible.
Your words may remind them to turn toward Jesus rather than away from Him.
And think about one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack with a Bible verse.
Someone you genuinely love.
Maybe a brother who has drifted from God.
A sister who is carrying silent grief.
A friend who has stopped praying.
A parent who has been burdened by regret.
Or someone who thinks their past is too dark for Christ to redeem.
One sincere share can place Scripture before someone who might never search for a Christian article on their own.
Read 1 Kings 21 and 2 Kings 9:21–26 together when you have time.
Then read Romans 3, Luke 15, and John 19–20.
Let Scripture itself deepen what this story has stirred in you.
We want this community to be a place where God's Word is taken seriously, Jesus Christ is exalted, and people are encouraged to grow beyond a momentary emotional response into faithful discipleship.
And for those who have been wondering how to help this ministry continue, there is another meaningful way to stand with us.
Scripture affirms the value of supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those who receive instruction in the Word should share good things with those who teach.
First Corinthians 9:14 recognizes the legitimacy of Gospel workers receiving support through Gospel ministry.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters deeply.
Your salvation cannot be purchased, and your generosity is not a payment for grace.
Your local church and the responsibilities God has entrusted to you should not be neglected.

You may choose to treat it as part of your voluntary giving toward Gospel work, while recognizing that biblical tithing and financial stewardship are matters Christians understand and practice within their church traditions and convictions.
No guilt.
No spiritual pressure.
Just an opportunity to participate in something you believe is worth supporting.
These items can become practical reminders of faith, encouragement for daily life, or thoughtful gifts that open conversations about Jesus.
It is ministry.
It is helping us continue to write, teach, share Scripture, and make Christian discipleship resources available.
That is important.
God's Word is not a luxury product.
And no one should ever feel excluded from spiritual encouragement because they cannot afford a monthly commitment.
But those who can and willingly choose to support make it easier for this work to continue and grow.
Pray for the people who will encounter these messages.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Tell someone what Jesus has done in your life.
Support faithful Gospel work in whatever responsible way God has enabled you.
Because the mission has never been to make a platform famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
And now, before you leave, return with me one final time to that field.
Picture the road to Jezreel.
The approaching chariots.
The king asking whether there is peace.
The sudden realization that danger is coming.
The bow drawn tight.
The arrow released.
The king collapsing.
And the body carried into Naboth's field.
Years earlier, a man had been murdered because a king wanted what was not his.
Now another king lay dead on the ground connected to that injustice.
The Lord had not forgotten.
But remember, that field is not the final destination of the biblical story.
The story of Scripture moves toward another place.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
A Savior crowned with thorns.
A body laid in a tomb.
And an empty grave.
At Naboth's field, we see the seriousness of God's judgment.
At Calvary, we see the astonishing cost of our redemption.
At the empty tomb, we see the victory of the risen Christ.
The warning is real.
The mercy is real.
And the invitation is still open.
So do not spend your life trying to protect a crown that cannot save you.
Do not build your identity on power, reputation, possessions, or the appearance of being righteous.
Do not let the fear of exposure keep you from the freedom of confession and repentance.
Come to Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him the pieces of your life that you cannot repair by yourself.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And let His grace begin writing what sin could never write for you.
Because the most terrifying thing is not that God remembers the sins we try to bury. It is to stand before Him still refusing the Savior who came to forgive them.
